title: Close reading of “Attention Is All You Need”: how attention alone made the Transformer the foundation of every large model
summary: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all run on the Transformer. This 2017 paper threw out recurrent networks and processed language with attention alone. We take it apart step by step—problem, formulas, experiments—with worked examples and self-tests, so by the end you can explain for yourself why it works.
ai_summary: In 2017, Google researchers introduced the Transformer at NIPS: instead of processing a sentence word by word in order, every word attends to the entire sentence at once. The core pieces are scaled dot-product attention (dividing by √dₖ to keep softmax from saturating), multi-head attention with 8 heads, sinusoidal positional encoding, and stacks of 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers. It scored 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, and trained in just 3.5 days on 8 GPUs. Limits: compute grows quadratically with sequence length, and generation is still word by word; English-to-French is reported as 41.8 in the abstract and tables but 41.0 in the body.
brief: Problem: recurrent networks have to compute one word at a time, cannot be parallelized, and distant words must relay information through every step in between.

Method: attention only. Each word uses a query to match every word's key, then pulls back values by weight; 8 heads each look at different things, and sinusoidal positional encoding adds word order back.
Result: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, including ensembles; the base model's training cost is only a fraction of its competitors'.
Impact: GPT, BERT, and today's large language models all build on this architecture; the quadratic compute problem it left behind is still an active research area.

paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
paper.org: Google Brain · Google Research · University of Toronto

cover.headline: A close reading of the original Transformer paper
cover.highlight: Reading a sentence with attention alone

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In 2017, eight researchers from Google Brain, Google Research, and the University of Toronto published this paper at NIPS 2017; the main body is only 10 pages. It introduced a neural network architecture called **Transformer**. Instead of reading a sentence one word at a time in order, every word “looks at” every other word in the sentence at once, then decides which ones to consult and how heavily. That “who to look at, and how much” mechanism is called **attention**.

The problem the paper tackled was specific: machine translation. The results were just as specific: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, including multi-model ensembles; the largest model trained in 3.5 days on a single machine with 8 P100 GPUs.

But its impact went far beyond translation. Today's ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all variants of the Transformer under the hood, and the T in GPT stands for Transformer. Read this paper, and you have the key to understanding every large model. What follows starts from “what problem does it solve,” takes the design apart piece by piece, then puts it back together.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Transformer = attention (every word looks at the whole sentence and pulls information according to relevance) + feed-forward network (each word is processed in place) + positional encoding (restores word order) + residual connections and layer normalization (makes many stacked layers trainable). Stack that layer cleanly six times.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If they're new to you, don't worry; these three are enough:
list: **Vector**: a list of numbers. The model represents a word's meaning as a list of numbers; words with similar meanings get similar numbers.
**Dot product**: multiply two lists element by element and add the results. The more the two vectors point in the same direction, the larger the dot product—roughly, the more alike they are.
**softmax**: turns a set of scores into proportions that add up to 1; higher scores get a larger share.

sections.h: Before the Transformer: why word-by-word reading hit a wall

blocks.p: Before 2017, translation models were dominated by **recurrent neural networks** (RNNs, and their improved variants LSTM and GRU). An RNN reads a sentence much like someone running a finger along the words: at word t, it holds a single memory hₜ, computed from the previous memory hₜ₋₁ and the current word.

The paper points out the fundamental problem: **you must finish one step before you can start the next**. You cannot parallelize computation within a single sentence, so longer sentences get slower; and with long sentences, memory limits how many sentences you can batch. GPUs are best at doing a huge batch of identical computation at once—RNNs make them wait in line.

The second problem is that long-range information has to pass through relays. For a subject at the start of a sentence to affect a verb at the end, the signal must be handed through the memory of every word in between; the farther it travels, the more it degrades. The paper measures this with **path length**: in an RNN, the signal travels O(n) steps between two positions n words apart.

Some researchers used convolutional networks to get parallelism (the paper compares ConvS2S and ByteNet), but a single convolutional layer only sees a few neighboring words. Connecting distant words requires stacking many layers: path length grows linearly with distance in ConvS2S and logarithmically in ByteNet.

Attention had existed since 2014, but almost always as an add-on to RNNs. This paper asked a bolder question: what if you throw away recurrence and convolution entirely and keep **only attention**? The title, “Attention Is All You Need,” is their answer.

fig.subtitle: Adapted from Table 1 of the paper; n is sentence length, k is convolution kernel width. The amber row is the self-attention used by the Transformer.
rows: No—must wait for the previous step
Looks at a small local window at a time

Every word directly looks at the whole sentence

plain.title: A game of telephone vs. a group chat
plain.text: An RNN is like a game of telephone (A): what person 1 says has to pass through 2, 3, and 4 to reach person 5, one at a time, and it degrades with each pass. Self-attention is like opening a group chat (B): everyone can talk directly to anyone else, in one step, and everyone can speak at once.

sections.h: What attention is: a weighted lookup

callout.title: Think of attention as a trip to the library
callout.text: You walk in with a question (**Query**). Every book has a label on its spine (**Key**), and the real content is inside (**Value**). You compare your question against each label; the better the match, the more attention that book gets. The answer you walk out with is a weighted blend of each book's content by how well it matched. In the Transformer, every word in a sentence plays all three roles at once: the asker, the label being compared, and the content being retrieved.

blocks.p: The paper defines attention in a single line: it maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output; the output is a weighted sum of the values, and each value's weight is determined by how well the query matches the corresponding key. The specific algorithm it uses is called **Scaled Dot-Product Attention**, written as:

formula.expr: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ ) · V

parts.desc: The query matrix: each row is what one word is “looking for”
The key matrix: each row is the label of what a word “can be found by”
The value matrix: each row is the information a word actually carries
Dot-product every query with every key to get a score table of “how related is this pair”
The square root of the key dimension dₖ; it shrinks the scores, for reasons explained in the next section
Turn each row of the score table into weights that add up to 1
Use those weights to average the values of all words into each word's new representation

formula.note: The whole process is just two matrix multiplications and one softmax—exactly the kind of computation GPUs are best at—so the entire sentence can be processed in one shot.

plain.title: Mixing a drink by proportions
plain.text: Each word holds a cup of “content” (value v). First compare query q with each word's key k to get scores; after softmax they become proportions that add up to 1. Then pour from each cup into a new one according to those proportions—in the figure, the hand-worked weights 0.51, 0.19, and 0.31. The resulting mix is the word's new representation.

blocks.p: Where do Q, K, and V come from? Each word is first represented as a 512-dimensional vector (d_{model} = 512 in the paper), then multiplied by three learnable matrices W^{Q}, W^{K}, and W^{V} to produce its own query, key, and value. Those three matrices are learned during training: the model figures out what each word should ask, what label it should expose, and what content it should hand over.

Now let's work through a tiny example by hand. Suppose the sentence is “cat sat on the mat,” and it is “cat”'s turn to query, with vector length dₖ = 4. The numbers are invented to keep the arithmetic easy:

fig.title: One hand-computed attention step: “cat” attends most to itself, then to “the mat”
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: vectors are invented for the demonstration, not paper data. Query q = [1, 0, 1, 0], dₖ = 4, so √dₖ = 2
fig.note: Output = 0.506×[10, 0] + 0.186×[0, 10] + 0.307×[5, 5] ≈ [6.6, 3.4]. In “cat”'s new representation, just over half the information comes from itself, and a good amount of “the mat” is mixed in.

blocks.p: Notice two things. First, the weights are **relative**: softmax only cares how far apart the scores are, not their absolute size. Second, the output is a **blend**: “cat”'s new vector no longer just represents “cat”—it represents “the cat that sat on the mat in this sentence.” Repeated across layers, each word's representation becomes increasingly context-aware.

callout.title: Attention is not “staring at just a few words”
callout.text: Many people assume attention simply highlights important words. It is actually a continuous weighted average: every word in the sentence gets seen, just with different weights; and the weights are not hand-written rules—they are learned from training data.

sections.h: Why divide by √dₖ: a key detail that is easy to skip

blocks.p: The √dₖ in the formula looks like a casual constant, but the paper gives it a dedicated footnote. It is key to understanding why attention trains at all.

The paper's derivation runs like this: assume every component of query q and key k is an independent random variable with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product q·k = q₁k₁ + q₂k₂ + … + q_{dₖ}k_{dₖ} is the sum of dₖ random variables. Its mean is still 0, but its **variance becomes dₖ**. In the paper each head has dₖ = 64, so the dot products have standard deviation √64 = 8, and scores routinely land in the teens or twenties.
When scores spread out that much, softmax becomes extreme: the largest score takes nearly all the weight and the others approach 0. Compare:

fig.title: Same relative scores, but scaling them by 8 makes softmax give almost everything to the top item
fig.subtitle: Illustrative calculation: the two rows have the same score ratios, but the second row is multiplied by 8

plain.title: Once gaps widen, winner takes all
plain.text: With scores 2, 1, and 0, the weights are still fairly spread out. Multiply all scores by 8—relative relationships unchanged—and softmax hands almost all weight to the top one. Fine-tuning then barely moves anything, and the model cannot learn. Dividing by √dₖ turns the score's volume down, preventing winner-take-all.

blocks.p: When weights are squeezed into nearly all 0s and 1s, softmax sits in a region of **very small gradients**: no matter how the model nudges its parameters, the output barely changes, so it gets no signal about which direction to change. Training stalls. Dividing by √dₖ pulls the dot product's variance back to 1 and keeps softmax in a range that is easy to learn from.

The paper also offers a comparison: the other common approach, “additive attention” (which uses a small neural network to compute match scores), beats **unscaled** dot-product attention when dₖ is large. Add the scaling, and dot-product attention is both fast—it can use highly optimized matrix multiplication—and just as good.

quiz.q: If you increase each head's dₖ from 64 to 256 but still divide only by 8 (that is, continue scaling by √64), what problem is most likely?
options: The dot-product variance increases 4×; softmax gets more extreme, gradients shrink, and training becomes harder
No effect; softmax only cares about relative scores
Attention becomes more uniform, with every word getting roughly equal weight
quiz.why: Using the paper's footnote derivation, the dot-product variance equals dₖ. Change dₖ from 64 to 256 and variance increases 4×; standard deviation goes from 8 to 16. If you still divide by 8, the scores remain twice as large as before, and softmax is more easily squeezed. The correct adjustment is to divide by √256 = 16. Option C is only half right: softmax does care only about relative scores, but scaling all scores up magnifies the relative gaps too.

blocks.p: Single-shot attention has a flaw: each word ends up as a weighted **average**, and averaging blends different kinds of relationships together. The word “it” both needs to know what it refers to (a coreference relationship) and what role it plays in the sentence (a syntactic relationship); one average struggles to hold both. The paper says plainly that with a single head, averaging inhibits this.

The paper's solution is **multi-head attention**: split the 512 dimensions into 8 slices of 64 (h = 8, dₖ = dᵥ = 64). Each slice gets its own set of W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V} and does attention independently; the 8 results are concatenated back to 512 dimensions and mixed by a matrix W^{O}. Because each head's width is one-eighth of the original, total computation is similar to one full-size single head—effectively seven extra experts for free.

formula.expr:
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, …, head₈) · W^{O}
headᵢ = Attention(Q·W_{i}^{Q}, K·W_{i}^{K}, V·W_{i}^{V})

parts.desc: Head i: use its own projection matrices to compress Q, K, and V to 64 dimensions, then run scaled dot-product attention
Concatenate the 8 heads' 64-dimensional outputs end to end, returning to 8 × 64 = 512 dimensions
Then multiply by another matrix to fuse the eight experts' opinions into one result

plain.title: Several judges, each covering a different area
plain.text: One attention pass can only produce one kind of “who to look at” average. Multi-head attention is like inviting several judges to read the same sentence at once: one focuses on what “it” refers to, one on grammar, one on neighboring words. At the end their opinions are concatenated, so information is not muddled by a single average.

fig.title: Two heads looking separately: head 1 tracks what “it” refers to; head 2 tracks the immediately preceding word
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not paper data. Each row is one word's attention distribution and sums to about 1; darker amber means more weight, and the amber-outlined row is “it”.
fig.note: Head 1: when reading “it,” most attention lands on “cat,” so the model infers that “it” refers to the cat (the hungry one is the cat, not the mouse).

fig.title: Head 2 shifts focus: nearly every word watches the word just before it
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not paper data

blocks.p: This is not our wishful interpretation. The paper's appendix actually plots attention heads from the trained model: in encoder layer 5, one head reaches across a long distance to link the verb “making” with the later phrase “more difficult”; two heads specialize in coreference, and when reading “its” they focus sharply on its antecedent “Law”; other heads visibly follow sentence structure. The paper's conclusion: different heads really do learn to do different things.

fig.title: Too few or too many heads both hurt: 8 and 16 heads are best
fig.subtitle: Units: BLEU on the English-to-German dev set (newstest2013), with total computation held constant. Amber is the paper's default of 8 heads.
fig.note: From group (A) in the paper's Table 3: more heads means fewer dimensions per head.

blocks.p: Single-head attention scores 0.9 BLEU below the best setting, but more heads are not always better. With 32 heads, each head is down to 16 dimensions and lacks expressiveness, so the score falls back to 25.4. 0.9 points may not sound like much, but remember that this paper's record-setting improvement was only about 2 points.

sections.h: Positional encoding: putting word order back without recurrence

blocks.p: Attention has a built-in blind spot: it **doesn't know order**. When each word looks at the whole sentence, it sees a pile of words and their content, with no information about who comes before whom. Without any fix, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are made of the same three words in the model's eyes and nearly indistinguishable. RNNs don't have this problem because they read in order by construction; remove recurrence and you have to add order back another way.

The paper's solution is to create a “position vector” for each position and **add** it directly to the word vector (both are 512-dimensional, so they can be summed). The position vectors are generated from sine and cosine functions at different frequencies:

formula.expr:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )

parts.desc: The word's position in the sentence: 0, 1, 2…
The dimension index. Even dimensions use sin, odd dimensions use cos, paired up.
Controls how slow the slowest wave is: wavelengths stretch from 2π all the way to 10000·2π.

callout.title: Like a clock with many hands.
callout.text: The second hand spins fast, the minute hand slower, the hour hand slower still. Looking only at the second hand, you can't tell 1 o'clock from 2 o'clock; combine several hands and you can uniquely identify a moment. The 512 dimensions of the positional encoding are like 256 pairs of hands running at different speeds—one sin and one cos per pair—so every position corresponds to a unique set of “hand readings.”

blocks.p: Why sine and cosine specifically? The paper's reason: for any fixed offset k, the encoding at position pos+k can be written as a **linear function** of the encoding at position pos. The angle-sum identities guarantee this, which makes it easy for the model to learn relative position relationships like “look 3 words ahead.”

The paper also tried the other approach: skip the formula and let the model learn a vector for each position directly. Results were nearly identical (25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU on the dev set). They chose the sinusoidal version because it may let the model handle longer sentences than seen during training, since the formula can produce an encoding for any position.

quiz.q: If you remove positional encoding entirely, what capability does the Transformer lose most directly?
options: It cannot distinguish word order; “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are hard to tell apart.
It cannot process sentences longer than 512 words.
quiz.why: Attention itself is insensitive to order; word order information is entirely supplied by positional encoding. Parallelism comes from attention's structure and has nothing to do with positional encoding; multi-head attention still works, it just doesn't know who comes before whom.

sections.h: Putting the pieces together: 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers

blocks.p: Like the mainstream translation models of the time, the Transformer is split in two: the **encoder** reads the source (say, an English sentence) and turns each word into a context-aware vector; the **decoder** uses those vectors to write the translation (say, German) one word at a time, each step taking the words already written as input to produce the next word. Both sides are stacks of 6 identical layers (N = 6).

fig.title: Inside one encoder layer, a word goes through four steps in order
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: every step outputs 512 dimensions, so the outputs can be added back and stacked layer after layer.

steps.name: Multi-head self-attention
steps.desc: Each word looks across the whole sentence and mixes in other words' information according to relevance.

steps.name: Residual + layer normalization
steps.desc: Adds the step's result back to the original input, then pulls the values back into a stable range.

steps.name: Feed-forward network
steps.desc: Each word separately passes through a small two-layer network with ReLU in between, processing the information it just collected in place.

steps.name: Residual + layer normalization
steps.desc: Add back to the input and normalize again, then pass it to the next layer.

parts.desc: Expands the 512-dimensional word vector to 2048 dimensions.
ReLU: negatives become 0, positives stay unchanged, adding nonlinearity to the network.
Then compresses it back to 512 dimensions.

formula.note: Every position uses the same set of parameters, but different layers have different parameters. The paper notes this can also be viewed as two convolutions with kernel size 1.

plain.title: Each word passes through the same machine once
plain.text: Attention handles information exchange between words; the feed-forward network is a small machine that each word passes through separately, without disturbing the others. All positions share the same machine (the same parameters), so they can be processed side by side at once.

blocks.p: **Residual connection** means “copy the input and add it to the output as is.” That way each layer only has to learn “how much to change on top of the original,” and signals and gradients can travel straight through many layers along this “shortcut,” avoiding the training stagnation that comes with too many layers. It comes from ResNet (2015), which the paper cites. **Layer normalization** pulls the values of each word vector back to around mean 0 and variance 1, making training more stable.
Each decoder layer has one more sublayer than the encoder, three in total:

list: **Masked self-attention**: words in the translation can only look at themselves and earlier words, never at later ones. The trick is to set scores for “future positions” to negative infinity before softmax; after softmax those positions get a weight of 0.

**Encoder-decoder attention**: queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder's output. In other words, each time it writes a German word, it goes back to “check” the entire English source sentence.
**Feed-forward network**: the same as in the encoder.

callout.title: Masking is like covering up the answers during a test.
callout.text: During training, the entire correct translation is fed in at once, so all positions can be computed in parallel; but each position has everything after it masked out, so it can only predict the next word from the preceding words, mimicking the real “write as you think” generation process. Today's large language models generate text with exactly this mechanism.

callout.title: Attention isn't the whole Transformer
callout.text: Count the parameters in one layer using the paper's sizes: the four attention projection matrices (W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}, W^{O}) total 4 × 512 × 512, while the feed-forward network has 2 × 512 × 2048—exactly twice as many, ignoring biases. That means roughly two-thirds of a layer's parameters live in the feed-forward network. Attention moves information between words; the feed-forward network processes each word in place. Both are essential.

blocks.p: Two final small design choices: the input and output share the same embedding matrix (the encoder embedding, decoder embedding, and the output layer's matrix for turning vectors back into words are the same), and the embedding is multiplied by √d_{model} before adding positional encoding.

sections.h: Why self-attention is better: the paper's three measures

blocks.p: Section 4 of the paper answers “why self-attention” with three measures: per-layer **computational cost**, how much can be parallelized (the minimum number of sequential steps required), and the **longest path** between any two positions. The comparison table earlier already gave the conclusion: self-attention connects any two words in a constant number of steps—the shortest path, and the best suited to parallelism.

Computational cost deserves a closer look. Self-attention costs n²·d per layer (n words compared pairwise, each comparison d dimensions); a recurrent layer costs n·d². Which is cheaper depends on whether the sentence length n or the vector dimension d is larger:

fig.title: When the sentence is shorter than the vector dimension, self-attention is cheaper; once the sentence grows long, it becomes far more expensive.
fig.subtitle: Illustrative estimate: d = 512, comparing only the order of magnitude of per-layer compute.

blocks.p: The paper points out that in translation tasks of the time, sentences represented as subwords were usually much shorter than 512, so self-attention was faster. But it clearly saw the other side: for very long sequences, one could restrict each word to attending to a neighborhood of r words (restricted self-attention), at the cost of increasing the longest path to O(n/r), and it lists this as future work. That n² problem later became the core challenge for the entire long-context research direction.

The paper also mentions a side benefit: attention weights can be inspected, making the model easier to interpret. The “who is looking at whom” figures in the previous section are drawn exactly this way.

quiz.q: Using the estimates in the table, when processing a long text of 4,000 subwords, self-attention's per-layer compute is roughly how many times the recurrent layer's?
quiz.why: The ratio of n²·d to n·d² is n / d = 4000 / 512 ≈ 7.8. Whenever the sentence length exceeds the vector dimension, self-attention is more expensive, and every time length doubles, its compute quadruples.

sections.h: How it was trained: 8 GPUs, from 12 hours to 3.5 days

list: **Data**: English-to-German used the WMT 2014 dataset, about 4.5 million sentence pairs, segmented into subwords with byte-pair encoding (BPE), with a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 subwords for English and German. English-to-French used a larger dataset: 36 million sentences and a vocabulary of 32,000 subwords. Each training batch contained about 25,000 source-language subwords and 25,000 target-language subwords.

**Hardware and time**: one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model took about 0.4 seconds per step and trained for 100,000 steps, 12 hours total; the large model took 1.0 seconds per step and trained for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days total.
**Regularization**: each sublayer's output was dropped out before being added back to the residual path; the base model used a dropout rate of 0.1. They also used label smoothing of 0.1.

blocks.p: The learning-rate schedule is carefully designed; the paper gives a formula:

formula.expr: lrate = d_{model}^{−0.5} · min( step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5} )

parts.desc: For the first 4000 steps the second term applies, and the learning rate rises linearly with the step number; afterward the first term applies, and the learning rate gradually falls as the inverse square root of the step number.

plain.title: Warm up first, then gradually slow down
plain.text: The learning rate is how large a step the model takes each iteration. For the first 4000 steps (the light region) it starts small and gradually increases, like warming up before a run; afterward it gradually decreases with step count, so the steps get steadier closer to the finish.

callout.title: Why warm up?
callout.text: At the start of training the parameters are random, and the model has no idea which direction to go. Taking large steps immediately makes it easy to “fall”—the loss oscillates wildly or even diverges. It starts with small tentative steps, gradually speeds up, and once the direction stabilizes it gradually shrinks the steps again. This “rise then fall” learning-rate curve later became almost standard practice for training Transformers.

callout.title: Label smoothing: deliberately keeping the model from becoming overconfident
callout.text: During training, the model is not asked to give the correct word a perfect score; instead it leaves a little probability for other words (the paper uses 0.1). The paper says this makes perplexity (a measure of how “certain” the model is) worse, because the model learns to be less sure of itself, but final accuracy and BLEU both improve.

blocks.p: A few more tricks at test time: the base model averages parameters from the last 5 checkpoints, and the large model from the last 20; translation uses beam search (beam size 4, length penalty α = 0.6), considering several candidate translations rather than greedily picking only the best word at each step.

sections.h: The report card: better, and much cheaper

callout.title: What BLEU measures
callout.text: The most common automatic metric for machine translation: it compares a machine translation with human reference translations and counts how many words and phrases overlap. The maximum score is 100; higher is better. A gap of a few points counts as a clear improvement in this field.

fig.title: English-to-German: even the Transformer base model beat every previous model, including multi-model ensembles
fig.subtitle: Units: BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German test set (newstest2014). Amber marks the Transformer.
fig.note: From Table 2 of the paper. Ensembling combines the outputs of multiple models; it is usually stronger than a single model but costs several times as much.

fig.title: Training cost: the Transformer base model used only a fraction of its competitors'
fig.subtitle: Units: ×10¹⁸ floating-point operations (English-to-German). Amber marks the Transformer; the paper estimates this as training time × number of GPUs × compute per GPU.
fig.note: For example, 23 means 2.3×10¹⁹. The base model's cost is about one-third of ConvS2S, yet it scores more than 2 BLEU higher.

blocks.p: On English-to-German, the large model reached 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 points above the previous best (ConvS2S ensemble's 26.36); even the base model (27.3) beat every published model and ensemble.

On English-to-French, the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8 BLEU, setting a new single-model record; but Section 6.1 of the body says 41.0. The paper does not explain the discrepancy, so it is worth noticing when reading, and when citing it is best to follow the table and note the difference. The paper also says its training cost was less than one-quarter of the previous best model's.

To show the Transformer is not just a translation model, the authors also applied it to **English constituency parsing**: they wrote a sentence's parse tree as a string of symbols and had the model “translate” into it. This task has outputs much longer than inputs and strong structural constraints. With only about 40,000 Wall Street Journal sentences for training, a 4-layer Transformer scored 91.3 F1; with additional semi-supervised data it reached 92.7, beating all previous methods except a specially designed grammar model (RNNG, 93.3), and with almost no task-specific tuning.

sections.h: Ablation experiments: which design choices actually matter

blocks.p: Table 3 of the paper runs a set of controlled experiments: change one thing about the base model at a time and see how the English-to-German dev-set score moves. This is the most reliable way to judge which design choices really matter.

fig.title: Change one thing at a time and watch how the score changes
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper, English-to-German dev set (newstest2013); the base model has BLEU 25.8 and 65 million parameters. The blue column is BLEU.
rows: Keys too short, making it harder to judge who relates to whom
Nearly identical to the sinusoidal version

blocks.p: Four conclusions from this table: multi-head attention really helps, but the number of heads should be moderate; too-small dₖ hurts quality, and the paper infers that judging match compatibility is not simple—a more complex compatibility function than dot product might be better; bigger models are better; and dropout is crucial for preventing overfitting.

callout.title: How to read an ablation table
callout.text: When a paper introduces several new design choices at once, ablation experiments tell you how much each one contributes. When reading a paper, start with the ablation table; it often tells you more than the final results about where the paper's real contribution lies.

sections.h: What it didn't solve, and what happened next

blocks.p: In its closing section, the paper is candid about what to do next, and those items happen to become the main threads of AI development in the following years:

list: **Long sequences are expensive**: self-attention's compute grows quadratically with sequence length. The paper suggests attending only locally; later sparse attention, efficient attention, and long-context techniques are all wrestling with that n².

**Generation is still sequential**: the decoder still writes one word at a time. The paper lists “making generation less sequential” as a research goal; today's large models still generate text token by token, and inference acceleration remains a hot direction.

**Extending beyond text**: the paper planned to apply the Transformer to images, audio, and video. A few years later, Vision Transformer (2020) cuts images into small patches and reads them as “words,” and the diffusion model DiT (2022) also adopted the Transformer.

blocks.p: The Transformer's encoder and decoder were later “split apart” and developed separately: encoder-only BERT (2018) excels at understanding, while decoder-only GPT models excel at generation. Today's large language models mostly use only the decoder half, with refinements in details such as where normalization is applied and how positional encoding is done, but the “attention + feed-forward + residual” skeleton is exactly the same as in this paper.

callout.title: What to read next
callout.text: These follow-up papers are all on our paper reading list: BERT, GPT-3, Vision Transformer, Scaling Laws... We'll cover each of them in depth, and finished ones will appear on the paper close-reading page.

sections.h: Check yourself: have you really absorbed it?

quiz.q: What is the most fundamental reason a Transformer can train much faster than an RNN?
options: All positions in the same sentence can be computed at once, without waiting for the previous word to finish
quiz.why: In an RNN, step t depends on the result of step t−1, so steps can only be computed in order. In self-attention, every word directly looks at the whole sentence, and the whole sentence can be computed in one matrix multiplication, making full use of the GPU's parallel power. The base model in the paper has 65 million parameters—hardly a small number.

quiz.q: In the decoder's “encoder-decoder attention,” where do the query (Q), key (K), and value (V) come from?
options: Q, K, and V all come from the encoder.
Q comes from the decoder; K and V come from the encoder's output.
Q comes from the encoder; K and V come from the decoder.
Q, K, and V all come from the decoder.
quiz.why: The decoder uses its own current state to ask (Q), and searches the encoder's representation of the source (K, V). This is the step in translation where each generated word checks back against the source sentence.

quiz.q: Why is the decoder's self-attention masked?
options: To prevent the model from peeking at later correct answers when predicting a position.
quiz.why: During training, the full correct translation is fed in at once. If later words were not masked, the model could directly “copy the answers” and never learn true word-by-word generation. The mask sets future positions' scores to negative infinity, so after softmax their weights become 0.

callout.title: After reading, you should be able to answer these five questions in your own words.
list: Why is the RNN slow, and why can self-attention be parallelized?
What are Q, K, and V, and how is one attention pass computed?
Why divide by √dₖ? What happens without it?
What problem does multi-head attention solve that single-head attention has?
Without recurrence, how does the model know word order?
